Chemicals, Gases and Photoresist

Chemicals, Gases and Photoresist, stage 3 of 15Next stage: 04 Lithography

In plain terms

Photoresist is a coating that changes wherever light hits it. A machine spins a coat of it, thinner than a soap bubble, across the wafer. Light shines through a stencil onto the coat, and a liquid wash then takes away the parts the light reached. What remains is a pattern, and the next machine cuts that pattern into the wafer beneath, a step called etching. A few hundred other gases and liquids lay down layers, strip them off and clean the wafer between steps. All of them have to be pure to about one stray metal atom in every trillion. A chipmaker approves each formula for one factory and one product at a time. A new supplier has to earn that approval from scratch, so adding a second supplier takes years. Japanese companies held 78 percent of world photoresist sales in 2023[2].

In short

In July 2019 Japan began requiring an export license for each contract to sell photoresist, hydrogen fluoride or fluorinated polyimide to South Korea[22]. Japan's hydrogen fluoride exports to South Korea then fell 87.9 percent, but its photoresist exports did not[22]. Production of all three chemicals rose inside South Korea[22].

China banned exports of the metals gallium, germanium and antimony to the United States in December 2024[26]. Germanium metal averaged $4,100 a kilogram in 2025, against $1,392 in 2023[29]. In November 2025 China suspended the ban until 27 November 2026[27].

Why substitution is possible
Photoresist is the light-sensitive coating that holds the printed pattern on the wafer. Each formula is approved for one layer of one product at one fab. So a new supplier has to develop its version together with the fab, one layer at a time. When Japan required individual export licenses for resist and two other chemicals sold to South Korea in 2019, South Korea imported more from the United States, Taiwan and Belgium. Output of the three chemicals rose at Korean firms and at Japanese companies' affiliates in South Korea. Some of the American supply may have been Japanese material shipped by way of the United States. Japanese resist exports to South Korea did not fall, possibly in part because Japan allowed three-year bulk licenses for some resist sales in December 2019.
Where China stands

In a January 2021 brief, Georgetown University's CSET found that China made no photoresist for extreme-ultraviolet printing and was still developing resist for 193 nm printing. At the time China held under 5 percent of the photoresist market. In March 2026 the Chinese resist maker Hubei Dinglong said China had yet to reach large-scale production of advanced resist for 248 nm, 193 nm or extreme-ultraviolet printing. In February 2026 the US Geological Survey put China's share of world production of primary low-purity gallium at 99 percent. Since August 2023 China has required licenses to export gallium and germanium. It banned their export to the United States in December 2024, and in November 2025 it suspended that ban until 27 November 2026.

Where the US stands

The American firms Entegris, Qnity Electronics and Air Products are strong in filters, containers, polishing slurries and gas delivery. In photoresist, American companies ranked a distant second to Japanese companies by sales in 2023. In 2021 JSR of Japan agreed to buy Inpria, an Oregon maker of resist for extreme ultraviolet.

A chip fab uses a few hundred chemicals and gases, and a shortage of any one of them can stop it. The French gas company Air Liquide alone supplies more than 200 molecules and roughly 50,000 cylinders a year[1].

How it works

The resist has to change only where the light lands. It also has to react fast enough for the scanner, the machine that projects the pattern, to expose each patch of the wafer in milliseconds.

Since the 1990s the standard has been chemically amplified resist. In resists for 248 nm and 193 nm light, a photon absorbed in the film can free an acid molecule, and nothing more happens until the wafer is baked. In the bake, each acid molecule sets off hundreds of reactions around itself that turn the film soluble, so a little light does a lot of chemistry. The wash then takes away the exposed film and leaves the rest. The 248 nm light comes from a krypton fluoride (KrF) laser. The 193 nm light comes from an argon fluoride (ArF) laser and shines through a layer of water, which sharpens the image.

That chemistry works less well with extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light (see Lithography). An absorbed EUV photon instead knocks electrons loose, and a cascade of lower-energy secondary electrons makes the chemical changes in the resist[3]. A 13.5 nm EUV photon carries about fourteen times the energy of a 193 nm one, so the same dose of light arrives as far fewer photons. With fewer photons, random variation in where each one lands matters more. It shows up as ragged line edges and missing contact holes, the small wells that join one layer of wiring to the next.

Resist makers responded with metal-oxide resists, which are built on clusters with a tin-oxide core and absorb more of the EUV light than chemically amplified resists[4]. In 2021 the Japanese resist maker JSR agreed to buy Inpria, an Oregon maker of these resists[5].

The other chemicals and gases put material on the wafer, take it off or keep it clean. Bulk gases arrive by the metric ton, specialty gases in grams. Silane gas carries the silicon for new layers into the chamber that holds the wafer. A plasma tears nitrogen trifluoride into charged fragments, which scrub the chamber walls clean between wafers. Hydrofluoric acid cleans the wafer itself. Polishing slurries grind each new layer flat before the next goes on.

Sputtering targets are slabs of pure metal. A plasma knocks atoms off them, and the atoms settle on the wafer as thin metal films, including the barrier and seed layers for copper wiring[6]. Electroplating then fills in the copper wiring itself[7]. Filters and wafer carriers keep contamination out.

Each resist class is made for one kind of lithography, such as EUV, ArF immersion, ArF, KrF or i-line[8].

Who makes it

In a January 2021 brief, Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) put Japan's share of the semiconductor photoresist market at 90 percent, citing a 2019 estimate[8]. The brief put most of the rest with US and South Korean firms[8]. In a December 2025 strategy presentation, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) published figures from a separate survey by Fuji Keizai, a Japanese market research firm[2]. That survey counts sales by company nationality and puts Japanese companies at 77 percent in 2021 and 78 percent in 2023, with American and South Korean companies next[2].

CSET's January 2021 brief lists five Japanese resist makers: JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, Shin-Etsu Chemical, Fujifilm and Sumitomo Chemical[8]. It also lists Dongjin of South Korea, the American firms DuPont, EMD Performance Materials and Inpria, and four Chinese firms[8]. Qnity Electronics, the former DuPont electronics business, says in its 2025 annual report that it offers lithography materials for every wavelength, including EUV[9]. In its 2025 annual report summary, the Chinese firm Hubei Dinglong said China had yet to reach large-scale production of advanced resist for 248 nm, 193 nm or EUV printing[10]. The firm also said three of its own resists for 248 nm and 193 nm printing had moved into stable volume supply[10].

A vehicle of Japan Investment Corporation, a state-backed fund, bought 84.36 percent of JSR's shares at ¥4,350 each in a tender offer that closed on 16 April 2024[11]. JSR's shares were delisted from the Tokyo Stock Exchange on 25 June 2024[12].

Tokyo Ohka Kogyo sold ¥139,668 million in the first half of fiscal 2026, up 25.1 percent, as strong demand for AI servers in data centers raised demand for chips[13]. Fujifilm planned to raise its polishing-slurry capacity at Kumamoto by about 30 percent from January 2025[14]. It also scheduled new production and quality-evaluation equipment for EUV resist at Shizuoka and Pyeongtaek to start in October 2025[15].

World sales of wafer fabrication materials reached $45.8 billion in 2025, and sales of packaging materials reached $27.4 billion[16].

In electronic gases, CSET named Merck, Air Products and Air Liquide as the market leaders in January 2021[8]. Air Liquide's electronics business sold €2,465 million in 2025, 9.1 percent of group revenue[1]. Smaller firms specialize in particular chemicals: SK Materials in nitrogen trifluoride, Kanto Denka in fluorine chemistry, and Stella Chemifa and Morita in ultra-high-purity hydrofluoric acid.

CSET's January 2021 brief, drawing on 2019 market reports, put five firms at more than 60 percent of the wet chemicals market[8]. It put DuPont and Cabot Microelectronics at about 56 percent of a $790 million market for polishing slurries[8]. Counting by company nationality, the same Fuji Keizai survey puts Japanese companies at 51 percent of polishing-slurry sales and 59 percent of high-purity cleaning-liquid sales in 2023[2]. Both shares were 49 percent in 2021[2].

Cabot Microelectronics renamed itself CMC Materials in October 2020[17]. The American firm Entegris completed its purchase of CMC Materials on 6 July 2022[18]. DuPont separated its electronics business into an independent company, Qnity Electronics, on 1 November 2025[19]. Qnity sells polishing slurries and pads[20].

In sputtering targets for semiconductors, JX Advanced Metals puts its own share of the world market at about 65 percent as of fiscal 2026[21].

The chokepoint

Supply at this stage has been disrupted three times since 2019, twice by governments and once by a war.

In July 2019 Japan put photoresist, hydrogen fluoride and fluorinated polyimide under individual export licenses for South Korea, so each export contract needed its own license[22]. Japan had supplied more than 90 percent of South Korea's imports of two of the three[22]. Its hydrogen fluoride exports to South Korea then fell 87.9 percent[22]. Japanese photoresist exports to South Korea did not fall, possibly in part because Japan allowed three-year bulk licenses for some resist sales in December 2019[22].

South Korea bought more hydrogen fluoride from the United States and Taiwan and more photoresist from Belgium[22]. Production of all three chemicals rose inside South Korea[22]. The rise came both from South Korean firms and from Japanese companies' affiliates in South Korea[22].

Researchers at Japan's Research Institute of Economy, Trade and Industry (RIETI) found that Japanese hydrogen fluoride exports to the United States rose[22]. They say some Japanese supply may have reached South Korea by way of the United States[22]. Japan ended the individual licenses on 23 March 2023, when it put exports of the three chemicals to South Korea under its bulk export license system[23].

In 2022 Russia invaded Ukraine, which supplied about 70 percent of the world's neon and 90 percent of the semiconductor-grade neon used by US industry[24]. Gas mixtures containing neon power the lasers in lithography scanners[24]. Many chipmakers had added to their gas stockpiles after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014[24]. Samsung, SK Hynix, Renesas and Rohm reported adequate neon supplies from China[24].

At this stage, China's export controls cover metals. On 3 July 2023 China announced that exports of gallium and germanium would need licenses from 1 August[25]. On 3 December 2024 it said it would in principle grant no licenses to export gallium, germanium, antimony or superhard materials to the United States[26]. On 9 November 2025 it suspended that ban until 27 November 2026[27].

The White House set out a trade deal with China on 1 November 2025[28]. Under it, China also agreed to issue general licenses for exports of gallium, germanium and antimony for the benefit of US end users and their suppliers[28].

In the United States, germanium goes mainly into fiber optics, infrared optics, semiconductors and solar cells, and radiation detectors[29]. Of the gallium used in the United States, 73 percent went into integrated circuits built on gallium arsenide or gallium nitride[30]. Another 26 percent went into optoelectronic devices such as LEDs and laser diodes[30].

Germanium metal averaged $4,100 a kilogram in 2025, against $1,392 in 2023[29]. US imports of the metal fell 67 percent in 2025 because of China's ban[29]. The US Geological Survey estimated that a total Chinese ban on gallium and germanium exports could cut US GDP by $3.4 billion[31].

A slower risk is the European Union's proposed restriction on PFAS, the long-lived fluorinated chemicals. These chemicals are used throughout a fab. The photoacid generators that free the acid in resist are fluorinated, and so are etch gases, chamber liners, pump seals and filter membranes.

The national authorities of Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden prepared the proposal and updated it after evaluating more than 5,600 comments[32]. ECHA, the EU chemicals agency, published the updated proposal on 20 August 2025[32]. The updated proposal assessed options that would let electronics and semiconductor makers keep using PFAS where the risks can be controlled[32].

In March 2026 ECHA's two scientific committees backed an EU-wide restriction with targeted derogations, or exemptions[33]. One committee gave its backing in a final opinion and the other in a draft, and their evaluation is due to finish by the end of 2026[33]. The European Commission will decide in consultation with the member states[32].

Key evaluation criteria

  • Purity, in parts per trillion of metallic contamination, a million times finer than parts per million. This requirement keeps new suppliers out.
  • Qualification lock-in: a resist or slurry is approved for one layer of one product at one fab, so switching suppliers means a new approval for every product that uses it.
  • Photon efficiency for EUV resists: how much light the resist absorbs sets the dose, and the dose sets how many wafers an hour the scanner prints. Too few photons per dose raise the defect rate, which is the argument for metal-oxide resists.
  • Transportability: bulk gases are often made on site at the fab, while specialty gases travel in cylinders and can be embargoed.
  • Byproduct exposure: gallium is recovered mostly as a byproduct of processing bauxite, the ore that aluminum is made from[30]. Germanium comes from certain zinc ores and coal deposits, so supply of both depends on another industry's economics[29].

Review questions

What does photoresist do?

It is a light-sensitive coating that holds the printed pattern, so the next step can etch that pattern into the wafer.

A wash removes the parts the light reached. The pattern that remains guides the etch. Reread: How it works

Which country makes most of the world's photoresist?

Japan.

Japanese companies held 77 percent of world sales in 2021 and 78 percent in 2023. Reread: Who makes it

Why does replacing a photoresist supplier take years?

Each formula is approved for one layer of one product at one factory.

A new supplier has to develop its version together with the factory, one layer at a time. When Japan put resist and two other chemicals under export licenses for South Korea in 2019, Korea bought more from other countries, and Korean firms and Japanese companies' affiliates in Korea made more. Some of the extra American supply may have been Japanese material shipped by way of the United States. Reread: The chokepoint

What does China control in this stage?

Exports of gallium and germanium, which have needed a license since August 2023.

Most gallium used in the United States goes into chips built on gallium arsenide or gallium nitride, and most of the rest into LEDs and laser diodes. On 9 November 2025 China suspended, until 27 November 2026, its December 2024 ban on selling gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials to the United States. Reread: The chokepoint
